newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU must match U.S. aerospace efforts-industry.
newsitem.headline: EU must match U.S. aerospace efforts-industry.

text.p: The European Union must adopt U.S.-style industrial policies for its aerospace sector if it is to fend off competition from its North American rivals, European industry association head Peter Fichtmueller told Reuters.

Fichtmueller, secretary general of the European Association of Aerospace Industries, said EU institutions should counter pressure from the United States by bolstering research into aerospace technologies and looking at the possibility of tax breaks and trade promotion efforts.

His remarks, made in an interview late on Thursday, came the day after European Commission President Jacques Santer announced a review of the European aerospace sector in the wake of draft Commission approval for Boeing Corp's merger with former rival McDonnell Douglas.
Santer said the Boeing case had highlighted the need to look at the effects of globalisation on EU industrial policy and its effects on the aerospace sector in particular.
"The Commission's move is most welcome because the European reaction cannot only be to put limits on American developments. It has to take up the challenge within our own field," Fichtmueller said.

The Commission, in return for anti-trust clearance of the deal, forced Boeing into a series of concessions including the scrapping of exclusive aircraft-supply deals with three carriers and the release of patent licensing rights arising from government-funded research.
"It's right that Europe has to get its act together with its own industry, which is a matter of industrial policy.
"Certainly the core issue at the present time is restructuring of European industry, which is nothing new.

"It's been a constant process through the past decades, initially on the national level, leading to consolidation or specialisation, and, since the 1990s increasingly also on cross-border restructuring and cross-border mergers," he said.

"In the midst of all this is certainly the issue of Airbus Industrie and the formation of a single corporate entity but equally, and on the back of that, the consolidation process will have to be extended to other sectors of the industry. That's commonly accepted.
"Any support from the Commission will be most helpful," he said, adding that its suggestions would add to some form of common, EU-level, policy on aerospace.
"Aerospace is a highly political matter. (U.S. President Bill) Clinton intervened personally in the Boeing matter which shows what dimension we are working in."

Fichtmueller said U.S. rivals enjoyed a double advantage over European companies in the shape of higher government funding for research and an amalgam of trade boosters in the form of tax breaks and export credit facilities.

"The U.S. side is fostering the competitive position of its industry financially, through tax and credit schemes, as well as what they describe as trade advocacy. Both are very under-developed in Europe compared to the U.S.," he said.
Fichtmueller added that while the Commission had a role in forming policy, real power to affect the industry lay with EU governments.

"It's clear, and nobody contests that, that any restructuring or merger can only be accomplished with the support of the governments concerned. Government support, both as customer and sponsor, is indispensable. In that sense, it's governments who are called to act," he said.
And there's the rub. Last Thursday's report in French-language daily Le Monde quoted French Defence Minister Alain Richard as saying that aircraft maker Aerospatiale should stay in the public sector.

Were that to prove true, experts see the much-touted marriage of Aerospatiale with private warplane maker Dassault Aviation being thrown into doubt along with plans for a wholesale restructuring of the four-nation Airbus consortium which includes Aerospatiale.
